newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian royalists gather strength for elections.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian royalists gather strength for elections.

text.p: Cambodia's co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh has stepped up efforts to win sole power at 1998 polls by turning to old friends, including the Khmer Rouge, to broaden his support, analysts said.

But the prince's main political rival, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, cannot stomach the prospect of an alliance against his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) and has lost little time taking steps to scupper any such plan, the analysts said.

The analysts believe Hun Sen was behind allegations by 10 self-proclaimed Khmer Rouge defectors on Saturday that opposition leader Sam Rainsy and his Khmer Nation Party (KNP) had been taking secret funds and support from the guerrillas since Ranariddh and Hun Sen formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-run elections in 1993.

Their leader Duong Buntha, reading from a statement after meeting Hun Sen, said his Phnom Penh-based undercover agents had first approached Ranariddh to defect and were told to keep quiet about Sam Rainsy's alleged ties to the outlawed rebel group.
Ranariddh called the men liars and Sam Rainsy said he had been slandered.

Analysts said there was no concrete evidence to support allegations against the KNP, which is seen by Hun Sen as a dangerous rival for partnership with Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party at the next scheduled elections in 1998.

"This is obviously related...to the possibility of the two parties forming a coalition against the Cambodian People's Party," said a Western political analyst. "It is clearly orchestrated by Hun Sen, and there's no doubt about that."
Hun Sen has made no comment on the Sam Rainsy case.

Differences between the two premiers broke into the open in March when Ranariddh, attempting to boost his party's flagging image, threatened to leave the government unless the CPP ceded more power to reflect FUNCINPEC's superior performance in the U.N.-sponsored election.
Hun Sen fuelled the tension by warning he would use force to prevent moves to dismantle the government and parliament.
Tempers cooled but the rivalry is resurfacing as the two parties vie to benefit most from massive Khmer Rouge defections since August.
Friction is likely to increase as the 1998 elections, which will return only one premier, draw closer.

Ranariddh told reporters earlier this month he would consider an alliance at the next elections with Sam Rainsy, a former ally who was expelled from FUNCINPEC and parliament last year after repeatedly criticising the government.

He has also moved to improve ties with former comrades-in-arms in the resistance alliance, including the Khmer Rouge and the faction headed by former premier Son Sann, which fought Hun Sen's communist government in the 1980s.

Vietnam installed the Hun Sen regime after invading Cambodia in late 1978, ending the Khmer Rouge's disastrous three-year rule during which more than one million people died from starvation, execution or disease.
The fighting ended after the four warring factions signed a peace pact in Paris in 1991.
"What we're seeing is a tendency toward a broad anti-CPP coalition which would gather all its (original) rivals...including the Khmer Rouge," said one Western analyst.
Sam Rainsy echoed the view, telling Reuters, "I think there will be a tendency, a trend to regroup all the former allies to counter the Hun Sen-led CPP."

Last week the prince flew to Phnom Malai, one of the two key bases of former top Khmer Rouge cadre Ieng Sary, who split with hardliners loyal to Pol Pot in August and formally joined the government with his forces in the northwest earlier this month.
"I feel very comfortable...I'm very comfortable with them," said the prince. He told reporters his party would also seek to improve relations with Son Sann.
Hun Sen, who has been trying with some success to recruit his own supporters among Khmer Rouge guerrillas independent of Ieng Sary, has railed at attempts to form an anti-CPP alliance.
"This is the campaign trail, demonstrating the tripartite coalition, demonstrating the thing Hun Sen fears most," a foreign guest commented during Ranariddh's tour last week.
